question: Under Rea 404.05, when a New Hampshire salesperson advertises property listed by their firm, what must every such advertisement clearly indicate?
choice_a: The square footage of every listed property
choice_b: That it is an advertisement of a principal broker
choice_c: The seller's asking price history
choice_d: The salesperson's personal cell phone number only
explanation: Rea 404.05 requires that advertisements clearly indicate they are the advertisement of a principal broker, preventing a salesperson from advertising as though offers originate from a private party or from the salesperson individually. Square footage and price history are not mandated ad content under this rule.

question: A New Hampshire salesperson wants to run a print ad for a listing without naming any brokerage firm or broker. Is this permitted under Rea 404.05?
choice_a: Yes, provided the ad runs for fewer than 30 days
choice_b: Yes, as long as the ad includes a photo of the property
choice_c: No, the ad must prominently include the name of the brokerage firm with which the licensee is associated, or the name of the licensee's principal broker
choice_d: No, but only if the property is a condominium
explanation: Rea 404.05 requires advertisements for others' property to prominently include the name of the brokerage firm the licensee is associated with, or the name of the licensee's principal broker. A photo or short run time does not satisfy this requirement.

question: Which of the following best describes a 'blind ad' violation under New Hampshire's advertising rule, Rea 404.05?
choice_a: An advertisement that lists the property on more than one website
choice_b: An advertisement that omits the property's street address
choice_c: An advertisement printed in black-and-white rather than color
choice_d: An advertisement structured so it appears offers of real property are being made directly by a principal (owner), rather than through a licensee
explanation: Rea 404.05 prohibits salespersons and brokers from advertising real property in a way that suggests the offer comes from the principal rather than a licensee; every ad must clearly show it is a principal broker's advertisement. Omitting a street address or using black-and-white print is not what the rule targets.

question: A New Hampshire associate broker operates under a team name on social media ads but never references her principal broker or firm. Which rule does this most directly violate?
choice_a: Rea 404.05, because ads must identify the brokerage firm or principal broker the licensee is associated with
choice_b: Rea 404.01, because no office sign was displayed
choice_c: RSA 331-A:16-a, because a managing broker vacancy was not filled
choice_d: Rea 701.03, because water supply information was omitted
explanation: Advertising identification requirements fall under Rea 404.05, which requires disclosure of the brokerage firm or principal broker's name. The other cited rules govern water supply disclosures, branch office vacancies, and office signage, none of which apply to a social media ad's content.

question: Under New Hampshire's advertising rule, does the medium of the advertisement (internet listing versus print flyer) change the identification requirements of Rea 404.05?
choice_a: Yes, print flyers are exempt but internet ads are not
choice_b: No, the same identification requirements apply regardless of the advertising medium used
choice_c: Yes, internet ads are exempt from any identification requirement
choice_d: Yes, only newspaper ads must name the brokerage firm
explanation: Rea 404.05 applies to advertisements generally and does not carve out an exemption based on the medium used; internet and print advertising are both subject to the same disclosure requirements. None of the other options reflect an actual exemption found in the rule.

question: A New Hampshire salesperson advertises a listing but fails to name the individual principal broker or business name under which she operates. Aside from Rea 404.05, which statutory provision also treats this omission as prohibited conduct?
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, X separately lists, as grounds for discipline, advertising without stating the name of the principal broker or business name under which the salesperson or broker operates (subject to a limited exception in RSA 331-A:16, IV(c)). RSA 331-A:13 concerns escrow accounts, RSA 331-A:16 concerns branch offices, and Rea 701.04 concerns insulation disclosure.

question: Before a New Hampshire principal broker may open a branch office, what must the principal broker do under RSA 331-A:16?
choice_a: File the application only if the branch is in a different county
choice_b: Simply notify existing clients by mail
choice_c: Wait until the branch has operated for 90 days, then register it
choice_d: Submit a branch office application form to the commission prior to opening the branch
explanation: RSA 331-A:16 requires the principal broker to submit a branch office application form to the commission prior to opening any branch office. There is no rule allowing after-the-fact registration, client-notice-only compliance, or a county-based exception.

question: Under RSA 331-A:16, who must the principal broker designate to direct, supervise, and manage each branch office of a New Hampshire brokerage firm?
choice_a: A managing broker who is a licensed real estate broker
choice_b: Any full-time employee, licensed or not
choice_c: A property manager licensed only in another state
choice_d: The firm's accountant
explanation: RSA 331-A:16 requires each branch office to be directed, supervised, and managed by a licensed real estate broker, and the principal broker must designate a managing broker for each branch. An unlicensed employee, an out-of-state-only licensee, or an accountant does not satisfy this requirement.

question: A New Hampshire salesperson transfers from a firm's main office to one of its branch offices. Who is responsible for notifying the commission of this internal transfer under RSA 331-A:16?
choice_a: The salesperson alone, with no broker involvement
choice_b: The principal broker
choice_c: The buyer in the salesperson's most recent transaction
choice_d: No notification is required for internal transfers
explanation: RSA 331-A:16 places responsibility on the principal broker to notify the commission when licensees transfer between branch locations within the same firm. The salesperson acting alone, a client, or no notification at all are not compliant options.

question: Under RSA 331-A:16, a corporate officer of a New Hampshire brokerage firm who actively engages in real estate brokerage activity on the firm's behalf must:
choice_a: Be exempt from licensure if serving without salary
choice_b: Hold a notary commission instead of a real estate license
choice_c: Hold an active broker or salesperson license
choice_d: Only sign as an authorized corporate signatory, with no license required
explanation: RSA 331-A:16 requires that corporate officers, partners, or association members who actively engage in real estate brokerage activity hold an active broker or salesperson license. Being an authorized signatory, holding a notary commission, or serving unpaid does not substitute for licensure.

question: A New Hampshire branch office's managing broker suddenly becomes disabled and can no longer serve. Under RSA 331-A:16-a, what may the principal broker do?
choice_a: Transfer all branch listings to the main office automatically with no notice
choice_b: Close the branch permanently within 48 hours
choice_c: Allow the branch to operate with no managing broker indefinitely
choice_d: Appoint a licensed temporary manager for the branch
explanation: RSA 331-A:16-a allows the principal broker to appoint a licensed temporary manager when a managing broker vacancy occurs due to death, disability, or a change in affiliation. Immediate closure, an automatic listing transfer, or operating indefinitely without a managing broker are not authorized under the statute.

question: Under RSA 331-A:16-a, within what maximum period must a New Hampshire brokerage firm appoint a permanent managing broker for a branch office after a vacancy occurs?
choice_a: One year from the date of the vacancy
choice_b: 30 days from the date of the vacancy
choice_c: Five years from the date of the vacancy
choice_d: There is no time limit under the statute
explanation: RSA 331-A:16-a permits a temporary manager to serve for a period not to exceed one year from the date of the vacancy, at which point a permanent managing broker must be appointed. Neither 30 days nor five years, nor an unlimited period, reflects the statute's actual deadline.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, I, obtaining a New Hampshire real estate license through which of the following is grounds for disciplinary action?
choice_a: Attending an accredited pre-licensing course
choice_b: Fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment
choice_c: Passing the licensing exam on a second attempt
choice_d: Applying for licensure while residing in another state
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, I lists obtaining or attempting to obtain a license by means of fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment as grounds for discipline. Taking an approved course, passing the exam on retake, or applying while living out of state are all legitimate, non-disciplinary circumstances.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, III, a licensee's guilty plea or plea of nolo contendere to embezzlement in another state:
choice_a: Is irrelevant unless the crime involved real estate directly
choice_b: Only counts if the licensee was sentenced to prison time
choice_c: Counts as a conviction for purposes of NH disciplinary action, even though the sentence was suspended
choice_d: Never counts because it occurred outside New Hampshire
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, III expressly provides that a plea of guilty or nolo contendere is treated as a conviction, and this includes cases where the sentence was deferred or suspended, and convictions in any state or federal court, not only New Hampshire. Actual imprisonment and a direct real-estate nexus are not required by the statute.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, IV, a licensee who distributes a flyer with false statements reasonably likely to induce a buyer to act may be disciplined if:
choice_a: The statements happen to later become true
choice_b: The buyer never actually saw the flyer
choice_c: The flyer was distributed more than one year before the transaction closed
choice_d: The licensee knew, or by reasonable care and inquiry could have known, the statements were false
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, IV applies where the licensee knew, or through reasonable care and inquiry could have known, that the statements, descriptions, or promises were false. Whether the buyer saw the flyer, the timing of distribution, or a later coincidental truth are not the statutory test.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, V, which of the following describes prohibited conduct involving a scheme where a party relies on a licensee's representation?
choice_a: Knowingly committing, or being a party to, material fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, conspiracy, collusion, trick, scheme, or device
choice_b: Referring a client to an attorney for legal advice
choice_c: Recommending a licensed home inspector to a buyer
choice_d: Disclosing a known material defect to a buyer
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, V prohibits knowingly committing, or being a party to, material fraud, misrepresentation, concealment, conspiracy, collusion, trick, scheme, or device upon which another person relies. Referring clients to professionals or disclosing known defects are proper practice, not violations.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, VI, a New Hampshire principal broker who continues to accept the services of a salesperson after that salesperson's license has been suspended is:
choice_a: Permitted to do so for a 60-day grace period
choice_b: Subject to discipline for accepting the services of a salesperson without a valid license
choice_c: Permitted to do so if the suspension is under appeal
choice_d: Permitted to do so as long as no commission is paid to the suspended salesperson
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, VI makes it grounds for discipline to accept the services of, or continue in a representative capacity with, a salesperson whose license has been revoked or suspended, or who was never licensed. Withholding commission, a pending appeal, or a supposed grace period do not create an exception under the statute.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, VII, if a New Hampshire licensee fails to return trust property within 30 days after the owner is entitled to it and makes demand, this failure is:
choice_a: Automatically forgiven if the licensee later returns the property
choice_b: Treated the same as a clerical filing error
choice_c: Prima facie evidence of conversion
choice_d: Only a civil matter with no bearing on licensure
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, VII states that failure to return money or other trust property within 30 days of a proper demand constitutes prima facie evidence of conversion, a disciplinary violation. A later return does not erase the presumption, and the statute treats this as more than a mere clerical matter.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, VIII, which of the following is grounds for discipline regarding trust funds?
choice_a: Using a trust account located at a federally insured New Hampshire institution
choice_b: Depositing trust funds within one business day
choice_c: Reconciling trust account records quarterly instead of annually
choice_d: Failing to promptly place trust funds in a proper trust account, or failing to reconcile records monthly
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, VIII makes it a violation to fail to promptly place trust funds in a proper trust account or to fail to reconcile records monthly. Prompt deposit, reconciling more often than annually, and using an insured NH institution all describe compliant conduct, not violations.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, IX, a licensee who refuses to produce trust account records for inspection when the commission demands them is subject to discipline because the statute requires licensees to:
choice_a: Disclose information and produce documents in the licensee's possession when the commission or its authorized representatives lawfully demand them
choice_b: Produce records only during a formal hearing
choice_c: Produce records only to the licensee's own attorney
choice_d: Produce records only when a court order is first obtained
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, IX makes it grounds for discipline to fail, upon demand, to disclose information or produce documents, books, or records in the licensee's possession for inspection by the commission or its authorized representatives. No prior court order or formal hearing is required to trigger this duty.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XI, a New Hampshire licensee who accepts a promissory note as earnest money instead of cash must:
choice_a: Convert the note to cash within 24 hours without telling anyone
choice_b: Communicate that fact in writing to the owner before the owner accepts the offer, show it in the earnest money receipt, and obtain the owner's written acknowledgment
choice_c: Simply inform the buyer that a note was accepted
choice_d: Do nothing further, since notes are treated identically to cash
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XI requires that acceptance of anything other than cash or its equivalent as earnest money be communicated in writing to the owner prior to acceptance of the offer, reflected in the earnest money receipt, and acknowledged in writing by the owner. Telling only the buyer, silently converting the note, or treating it as identical to cash all fail to meet this disclosure duty.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XII, a New Hampshire licensee who wants to act as a dual agent for both buyer and seller must obtain written consent:
choice_a: Verbally, since written consent is not required
choice_b: At closing, once the transaction is finalized
choice_c: From all parties at the time the dual agency relationship occurs, but no later than the preparation of a written offer
choice_d: Only from the seller, since the seller pays the commission
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XII requires full disclosure and written consent of all parties to the anticipated transaction at the time the dual agency relationship occurs, and no later than the preparation of a written offer. Obtaining consent from only one party, waiting until closing, or relying on verbal consent all violate this requirement.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XIII, a New Hampshire licensee who receives an undisclosed rebate from a contractor for referring repair work to the principal's property is:
choice_a: Permitted to keep the rebate if the amount is under $100
choice_b: Only required to report the rebate on the licensee's personal tax return
choice_c: Permitted to keep the rebate as long as the repair was completed satisfactorily
choice_d: Subject to discipline for accepting an undisclosed commission, rebate, or direct profit on expenditures made for the principal
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XIII prohibits accepting, taking, or charging any undisclosed commission, rebate, or direct profit on expenditures made for the principal. There is no dollar threshold exception, and satisfactory repair work does not excuse the nondisclosure; a personal tax filing does not cure the licensing violation.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XVII, a New Hampshire licensee who refuses to show a rental listing to prospective tenants because of their national origin has:
choice_a: Engaged in discrimination prohibited by the statute, which is grounds for disciplinary action
choice_b: Acted lawfully, since national origin is not a protected category under the statute
choice_c: Acted lawfully, since RSA 331-A:26 covers only sale transactions, not rentals
choice_d: Only violated federal law, not New Hampshire law
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XVII makes it grounds for discipline to discriminate against any person in hiring or in sales activity on the basis of race, color, creed, or national origin, or to violate any state or federal antidiscrimination law; this applies to sales activity broadly, not just sale transactions. National origin is explicitly listed, and the statute independently makes such discrimination a New Hampshire licensing violation, not merely a federal one.

question: A New Hampshire licensee is listing a single-family home served by a private well. Under Rea 701.03, what information must the licensee obtain from the seller about the water supply?
choice_a: Only the well's GPS coordinates
choice_b: The system type, its location, any malfunctions, the installation date, recent water tests, and any problems experienced
choice_c: Only whether the seller has ever consumed the water
choice_d: Only the name of the well-drilling contractor
explanation: Rea 701.03 requires the licensee to obtain seller information about the private water supply system's type, location, malfunctions, installation date, recent water tests, and problems experienced. GPS coordinates, personal consumption history alone, or only the contractor's name do not satisfy the rule's scope.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.03 (Private Water Supply Disclosure)

question: Under Rea 701.03, when must private water supply information be conveyed, in writing, to a buyer of a one- to four-family dwelling?
choice_a: Only after the home inspection is complete
choice_b: Only at the closing table
choice_c: Prior to or during the preparation of an offer
choice_d: Within 60 days after closing
explanation: Rea 701.03 requires that private water supply information be conveyed in writing to a buyer prior to or during the preparation of an offer, so the buyer has it before committing to purchase terms. Waiting until inspection, closing, or after closing comes too late under the rule.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.03 (Private Water Supply Disclosure)

question: Does the Rea 701.03 private water supply disclosure requirement apply to a listing for a five-unit apartment building?
choice_a: No, because private water supplies are banned statewide
choice_b: Yes, it applies to buildings of any size
choice_c: Yes, but only if the building is owner-occupied
choice_d: No, Rea 701.03 applies to one- to four-family dwellings, not five-or-more-unit buildings
explanation: Rea 701.03 is limited to one- to four-family dwellings with private water supplies; a five-unit apartment building falls outside that scope. There is no owner-occupancy carve-in, and private water supplies are not banned in New Hampshire.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.03 (Private Water Supply Disclosure)

question: A New Hampshire buyer later discovers the licensee never provided any written information about the seller's private well, despite the licensee knowing about a past malfunction. Which rule was most likely violated?
choice_a: Rea 701.03, requiring written conveyance of private water supply information to the buyer prior to or during offer preparation
choice_b: Rea 702.02, requiring immediate delivery of funds to the principal broker
choice_c: RSA 331-A:16, requiring branch office registration
choice_d: Rea 404.01, requiring an office sign
explanation: Failing to convey known private water supply information, including a past malfunction, in writing before or during offer preparation violates Rea 701.03. The other cited provisions govern unrelated topics: office signage, branch office registration, and delivery of client funds.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.03 (Private Water Supply Disclosure)

question: Under Rea 701.04, a New Hampshire licensee listing a three-family home must request from the seller:
choice_a: The R-value warranty certificate from the original builder only
choice_b: The type and location of the home's insulation
choice_c: A copy of the seller's utility bills for the past 5 years
choice_d: Nothing, because insulation disclosure is not required in New Hampshire
explanation: Rea 701.04 requires licensees to request the type and location of insulation from the seller for one- to four-family dwellings, which includes a three-family home. A builder's warranty certificate, past utility bills, or the assumption that no disclosure applies are not what the rule requires.

question: Under Rea 701.04, once a licensee obtains insulation type and location information from the seller of a one- to four-family dwelling, what must the licensee do with it?
choice_a: File it with the New Hampshire Real Estate Commission
choice_b: Disclose it verbally only, after closing
choice_c: Convey it in writing to the buyer prior to or during the preparation of an offer
choice_d: Retain it in the licensee's personal files with no obligation to share it
explanation: Rea 701.04 requires the insulation information to be conveyed in writing to the buyer prior to or during preparation of an offer, mirroring the timing requirement used for private water supply and sewage disclosures. Filing with the commission, only verbal post-closing disclosure, or simply retaining the information privately does not satisfy the rule.

question: Which New Hampshire disclosure requirement is distinctive because many other states do not require it, focusing specifically on a dwelling's thermal insulation?
choice_a: RSA 331-A:13's escrow account requirement
choice_b: RSA 331-A:16's branch office requirement
choice_c: Rea 404.01's office sign requirement
choice_d: Rea 701.04's insulation disclosure requirement
explanation: Rea 701.04 is New Hampshire's specific insulation disclosure rule, a requirement that is not universal among states and is a hallmark of New Hampshire's state-specific disclosure scheme. The other listed provisions concern escrow accounts, office signage, and branch offices, none of which relate to insulation.

question: A New Hampshire licensee lists a single-family home and, during offer preparation, gives the buyer a written statement describing the attic and wall insulation type and location. This satisfies which rule?
choice_d: RSA 331-A:26, XI
explanation: Providing written insulation type and location information to the buyer during offer preparation satisfies Rea 701.04, the insulation disclosure rule. Rea 701.05 concerns sewage disposal, Rea 404.03 concerns delivering copies of executed instruments, and RSA 331-A:26, XI concerns non-cash earnest money.

question: Under Rea 701.05, when listing a home with a private septic system, a New Hampshire licensee must obtain from the seller information about the system's:
choice_a: Resale value compared to municipal sewer connections
choice_b: Location, malfunction history, servicing dates, and contractor information
choice_c: Manufacturer's marketing brochure
choice_d: Original purchase price of the septic tank only
explanation: Rea 701.05 requires the licensee to obtain information about the private sewage disposal system's location, malfunction history, servicing dates, and contractor information. Resale value comparisons, a purchase price, or a brochure are not part of the rule's required content.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.05 (Sewage Disposal System Disclosure)

question: Under Rea 701.05, sewage disposal system information gathered from the seller must be conveyed to the buyer:
choice_a: Verbally, at the final walkthrough
choice_b: In writing, but only if the buyer specifically requests it
choice_c: In writing, prior to or during the preparation of an offer
choice_d: There is no timing requirement under the rule
explanation: Rea 701.05 requires that sewage disposal system information be provided in writing to the buyer prior to or during preparation of an offer, consistent with the timing used for water supply and insulation disclosures. A verbal walkthrough disclosure, a buyer-request trigger, or no timing requirement at all misstates the rule.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.05 (Sewage Disposal System Disclosure)

question: A New Hampshire seller mentions to the listing licensee that the septic system was pumped and serviced twice last year due to backups. Under Rea 701.05, the licensee must:
choice_a: Wait until after the home inspection to mention it, if at all
choice_b: Keep the information confidential unless the buyer's attorney formally requests it
choice_c: Disclose it only if the home is listed above a certain price point
choice_d: Obtain the servicing dates and malfunction history and convey them in writing to the buyer before or during offer preparation
explanation: Rea 701.05 requires the licensee to obtain the septic system's malfunction history and servicing dates and convey that information in writing to the buyer prior to or during offer preparation. Withholding it pending an attorney request, tying disclosure to price, or delaying until after inspection all violate the rule's timing and disclosure duty.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 701.05 (Sewage Disposal System Disclosure)

question: Rea 701.03, 701.04, and 701.05 collectively require New Hampshire licensees to obtain and convey seller information in writing to the buyer, prior to or during preparation of an offer, regarding which three subjects?
choice_a: Private water supply, insulation, and sewage disposal system
choice_b: Radon levels, lead paint, and asbestos
choice_c: Mineral rights, easements, and zoning variances
choice_d: Property tax history, HOA fees, and flood zone status
explanation: New Hampshire's Rea 701.03, 701.04, and 701.05 specifically address private water supply, insulation, and sewage disposal system disclosures. Radon/lead/asbestos, tax/HOA/flood status, and mineral rights/easements/zoning are addressed elsewhere, if at all, not under these three rules.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XVIII, a New Hampshire principal broker must keep records of escrow and trust accounts pertaining to entrusted funds for how long, and showing what information?
choice_a: 7 years, showing only the buyer's name
choice_b: 3 years, showing the date deposited, date of withdrawal, to whom paid, and other pertinent information the commission may require
choice_c: 1 year, showing only the total dollar amount deposited
choice_d: There is no specific retention period required
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XVIII requires records of escrow and trust accounts to be kept for 3 years, showing the date deposited, date of withdrawal, to whom paid, and other pertinent information the commission may require. A 1-year or 7-year period, or no period at all, misstates the statute.

question: Under RSA 331-A:26, XIX, a New Hampshire principal broker must preserve records relating to any real estate transaction for how long following its consummation?
choice_a: 10 years
choice_b: Indefinitely, with no allowed disposal
choice_c: 3 years
choice_d: 6 months
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XIX requires a principal broker to preserve transaction records for 3 years following the transaction's consummation. Neither 6 months, 10 years, nor an indefinite retention duty reflects the statutory requirement.

question: Under Rea 404.03, when a New Hampshire licensee obtains a fully executed purchase and sale agreement, what must the licensee do with respect to the parties?
choice_a: Release it only if a party pays a copying fee
choice_b: Hold the document for 90 days before releasing it to any party
choice_c: Send it only to the party's attorney, never to the party directly
choice_d: Deliver originals or copies of the executed instrument to the parties without delay
explanation: Rea 404.03 requires licensees to deliver originals or photocopies/electronic copies of executed instruments to the parties without delay when the instruments pertain to a transaction in which the licensee participated. Withholding for 90 days, charging a copying fee, or routing only through an attorney are not permitted under the rule.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 404.03 (Copies of Written Instruments)

question: A New Hampshire buyer's agent negotiates a lease on the buyer's behalf and the lease is fully executed. Under Rea 404.03, what is the agent's obligation regarding the lease document?
choice_a: Deliver an original or copy of the executed lease to the parties without delay, since it pertains to a lease transaction in which the licensee participated
choice_b: Deliver the lease only if requested in writing by the landlord
choice_c: No obligation exists because Rea 404.03 covers only sale transactions
choice_d: Deliver the lease only after the first month's rent is paid
explanation: Rea 404.03 applies to lease/purchase/sale/exchange transactions and other real estate transactions in which the licensee participates, requiring delivery of the executed instrument without delay; a lease transaction is expressly covered. A written request, a rent-payment trigger, or a false 'sales only' limitation are not accurate under the rule.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 404.03 (Copies of Written Instruments)

question: A New Hampshire commission investigator asks a principal broker to produce escrow account records from a transaction that closed two years and eight months ago. Must the broker comply?
choice_a: Yes, but only if the investigator has a court subpoena
choice_b: Yes, because RSA 331-A:26, XVIII requires escrow and trust account records to be retained for 3 years
choice_c: No, because escrow records need not be retained once a transaction closes
choice_d: No, because the retention period is only 2 years
explanation: Because RSA 331-A:26, XVIII requires escrow and trust account records to be kept for 3 years, records from a transaction that closed two years and eight months earlier must still be retained and produced. A 2-year period, no retention duty, or a subpoena requirement are inconsistent with the statute and with RSA 331-A:26, IX's demand-based production duty.

question: Which of the following is a distinction between RSA 331-A:26, XVIII and RSA 331-A:26, XIX?
choice_a: XVIII applies only to salespersons, while XIX applies only to principal brokers, with no retention period specified in either
choice_b: There is no meaningful distinction; the two subsections are identical
choice_c: XVIII covers escrow and trust account records, while XIX covers records relating to any real estate transaction generally, both with a 3-year retention period
choice_d: XVIII requires permanent retention, while XIX requires only 90-day retention
explanation: RSA 331-A:26, XVIII specifically addresses escrow and trust account records (date deposited, date of withdrawal, to whom paid), while XIX addresses a principal broker's duty to preserve records relating to any real estate transaction generally; both carry a 3-year retention period. The other answer choices misstate who each subsection applies to and the retention periods involved.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, a New Hampshire principal broker's escrow account must be maintained:
choice_a: In cash on the premises of the brokerage office
choice_b: At any financial institution located anywhere in the United States
choice_c: Combined with the broker's personal checking account for simplicity
choice_d: Separate and apart from the individual or office account, in an insured New Hampshire financial institution
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 requires the escrow account to be maintained separate and apart from the individual or office account, at an insured financial institution in New Hampshire. Combining it with a personal account, using an out-of-state institution, or keeping cash on premises would all violate the statute's separation and institution requirements.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, once a contract is fully executed, earnest money deposits and down payments received must be:
choice_a: Promptly deposited into the escrow account
choice_b: Deposited only after the buyer's mortgage is approved
choice_c: Converted to a certified check and mailed to the seller immediately
choice_d: Held by the salesperson personally until closing
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 requires that upon acceptance and execution of a contract, earnest money deposited and down payments received be promptly deposited into the escrow account. Personal retention by a salesperson, waiting for mortgage approval, or sending funds directly to the seller before closing all violate the statute.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, a New Hampshire broker's own personal or business funds may be placed in the escrow account only to cover:
choice_a: Marketing and advertising expenses
choice_b: Bank service charges or minimum balance requirements
choice_c: Payroll for unlicensed administrative staff
choice_d: The broker's monthly office rent
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 restricts the broker's own funds in the escrow account to amounts necessary to cover bank service charges or minimum balance requirements, guarding against commingling. Office rent, marketing costs, or payroll are personal/business expenses that must not be funded from the escrow account.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, interest earned on an interest-bearing escrow account generally accrues to whom, absent a different written agreement?
choice_a: The New Hampshire Real Estate Commission
choice_b: The listing agent's brokerage firm, split evenly with the seller
choice_c: The party making the deposit, as a sum to be used toward the purchase price
choice_d: The principal broker, as compensation for holding the funds
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 provides that interest earned accrues to the party making the deposit, as a sum to be used toward the purchase price, unless otherwise agreed in writing. The broker, the commission, and the listing brokerage are not the default recipients of that interest.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, when a real estate transaction becomes disputed and remains unresolved for more than 90 days, escrow funds may generally be withdrawn through which process?
choice_a: Automatic forfeiture to the brokerage firm
choice_b: The broker's unilateral decision, without notifying either party
choice_c: A verbal agreement between the buyer's and seller's agents
choice_d: A formal certified mail release process
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 permits withdrawal, after 90 or more days without resolution, through a formal certified mail release process, in addition to withdrawal upon contract performance, written agreement of all parties, or court order. A broker's unilateral decision, a verbal agent-to-agent agreement, or automatic forfeiture to the firm are not authorized withdrawal methods.

question: Under RSA 331-A:13, upon licensure a New Hampshire principal broker must sign a permit authorizing the commission to:
choice_a: Audit the escrow account or accounts
choice_b: Set the broker's commission split with salespersons
choice_c: Approve every advertisement before publication
choice_d: Co-sign every purchase and sale agreement
explanation: RSA 331-A:13 requires the broker, upon licensure, to sign a permit giving the commission permission to audit the escrow account or accounts, supporting the commission's oversight function. Setting commission splits, pre-approving ads, or co-signing contracts are not functions granted by this permit.

question: Under Rea 702.02, when a New Hampshire salesperson or associate broker receives client funds, what must the licensee do with those funds?
choice_a: Deposit them into the salesperson's personal bank account temporarily
choice_b: Immediately deliver them to their managing or principal broker
choice_c: Hold them until the end of the month, then reconcile and deliver
choice_d: Deliver them directly to the title company, bypassing the broker
explanation: Rea 702.02 requires that all monies received by a salesperson or associate broker be immediately delivered to their managing or principal broker. Depositing into a personal account, delaying until month's end, or bypassing the broker entirely all violate this rule.

question: Under Rea 702.01, every New Hampshire principal broker must maintain a trust account that is:
choice_a: Combined with the firm's general operating account for administrative ease
choice_b: Maintained at an out-of-state institution to simplify multistate transactions
choice_c: Separate and distinct from the broker's own account, held at a financial institution in New Hampshire
choice_d: Optional, unless the broker handles more than 10 transactions per year
explanation: Rea 702.01 requires every principal broker to maintain a separate escrow or real estate trust account, distinct from the broker's own account, at a New Hampshire financial institution. Combining accounts, treating the requirement as optional based on transaction volume, or using an out-of-state institution are not compliant.

question: Under Rea 404.01, a New Hampshire broker's office sign identifying the office as a real estate business must be displayed:
choice_a: Only inside the office, never visible from the street
choice_b: Nowhere, since office signage is prohibited statewide
choice_c: Only at the firm's main office, never at branch locations
choice_d: Outside the office, provided local zoning ordinances permit it
explanation: Rea 404.01 requires a sign identifying the office to be displayed outside the office, subject to local zoning ordinances permitting it. Requiring the sign to stay indoors, banning signage altogether, or exempting branch offices are not accurate statements of the rule.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 404.01 (Sign on Office)

question: Under Rea 404.02, a New Hampshire licensee who moves and changes their residential address must report the change to the commission within how many days?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 1 day
choice_c: There is no deadline
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: Rea 404.02 requires licensees to report changes such as address, phone, email, legal name, or trade name to the commission within 10 days, either through the online portal or by submitting the appropriate amendment forms. A 60-day window, a same-day requirement, or no deadline at all misstate the rule.

question: Under Rea 404.02, which of the following changes must a New Hampshire licensee report to the commission?
choice_a: Only changes to the licensee's social media handles
choice_b: Current address, phone number, email, work locations, legal name, and trade name
choice_c: Only the licensee's preferred pronouns
choice_d: Only changes to the licensee's vehicle used for business
explanation: Rea 404.02 requires licensees to keep the commission informed of current address, phone number, email, work locations, legal name, and trade name. Vehicle information or social media handles are not items the rule requires reporting.

question: Under Rea 404.02, when a licensee joins a New Hampshire principal broker, the principal broker's attestation confirms that the licensee will:
choice_a: Be an independent contractor exempt from any broker supervision
choice_b: Work exclusively from the licensee's home, with no principal broker oversight
choice_c: Be employed by or otherwise under contract with the principal broker to perform real estate licensee services
choice_d: Not require any written agreement with the principal broker
explanation: Rea 404.02 includes a principal broker attestation that the applicant will be employed by, or otherwise under contract with, the principal broker to perform services as a real estate licensee. Claiming exemption from supervision, exclusive home-based work with no oversight, or no written agreement contradicts this attestation requirement.

question: A New Hampshire principal broker relocates the firm's main office to a new street address. Which two rules together govern the broker's obligations regarding notifying the commission and displaying signage at the new location?
choice_a: RSA 331-A:26, VII and RSA 331-A:26, VIII
choice_b: RSA 331-A:13 and RSA 331-A:16-a
choice_c: Rea 701.03 and Rea 701.05
choice_d: Rea 404.02 (reporting the address change within 10 days) and Rea 404.01 (displaying an office sign outside, subject to local zoning)
explanation: Relocating the main office implicates Rea 404.02's 10-day address-change reporting duty and Rea 404.01's requirement to display an identifying sign outside the office, subject to local zoning. Escrow account and branch vacancy statutes, water/sewage disclosure rules, and trust conversion/trust fund provisions do not govern office relocation notice or signage.
source_note: N.H. Admin. Rules, Rea 404.01 and Rea 404.02
